entries.english:
He was reading in the Torah. The passage of the recitation of the Shema.

And the time arrived. The time for reciting the Shema.

If he directed his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation. According to the one who says that commandments require intention, this must be explained as meaning that he directed his heart to intend to fulfill his obligation. The one who says that commandments do not require intention explains it as meaning that he directed his heart to read according to the vowel signs and the proper rules, excluding one who reads to proofread: he does not read the words according to their vowel signs, but reads them according to their written form in order to understand the defective and plene spellings. Through such a reading he has not fulfilled his obligation. We hold in accordance with the one who says that commandments require intention.

At the breaks between sections. Further on, the Mishna explains what the sections are.

He may initiate a greeting out of respect. He may greet an honored person whom it is proper to greet first, such as his father, his teacher, or someone greater than himself in wisdom.

And may reply. It need not be said that he may return their greeting if they greeted him first.

And in the middle. Of the section.

He may initiate a greeting out of fear. To a person of whom he is afraid, lest that person kill him; and it need not be said that he may return that person's greeting. But not out of respect.

Rabbi Yehudah says: In the middle. Of the section, he may greet someone whom he fears, and return the greeting of someone whom he is obliged to honor.

And reply to anyone's greeting. If that person greeted him first. The halacha follows Rabbi Yehudah. Wherever it is forbidden to interrupt, it is just as forbidden to speak in the holy tongue as in other languages.

notes.he: כוונה לצאת ידי חובה אינה זהה לריכוז במילות הקריאה. הפירוש מציג שתי הבנות למשנה, ולבסוף פוסק שמצוות צריכות כוונה.
notes.en: Intention to fulfill an obligation is not identical with concentration on the words. The commentary offers two readings of the Mishna and concludes that commandments require intention.

entries.english:
Between ‘And He said’ and ‘True and firm’ he must not interrupt. For it is written, ‘But Hashem God is truth’ (Yirmeya 10); therefore one does not interrupt between ‘I am Hashem your God’ and ‘True.’ And this is the halacha.

‘And it shall be, if you listen’ applies both by day and by night. For it is written in it (Devarim 11), ‘You shall teach them to your children,’ and Torah study applies both by day and by night.

‘And He said’ applies only by day. For it contains the passage about fringes, which does not apply at night, as it is written (Bamidbar 15), ‘You shall see it.’

notes.he: המילה שאינה מוסבת על מצוות ציצית. בפירוש למשנה האחרונה בפרק הקודם נאמר שפרשת ציצית נאמרת גם בלילה בגלל הזכרת יציאת מצרים.
notes.en: “Which does not apply” refers to the commandment of fringes. The commentary on the preceding chapter’s final Mishna says that its passage is also recited at night because it mentions the Exodus.

entries.english:
Rabbi Yoasai says: He has not fulfilled his obligation. For it is written, ‘Hear’: make audible to your ear what you bring out of your mouth. The first teacher holds: ‘Hear’—in any language that you understand. The halacha follows the first teacher.

And he was not precise in its letters. To articulate them properly with his lips: in two words where the second word begins with the letter with which the first word ends, such as ‘upon your heart,’ ‘grass in your field,’ and ‘you will perish quickly,’ if he does not leave a space between them to separate them, he ends up reading those two letters as one letter.

Rabbi Yoasai says: He has fulfilled his obligation. The halacha follows Rabbi Yoasai. Nevertheless, at the outset one must be precise in its letters. Likewise, he must take care not to silence a mobile [sheva] or vocalize a silent one, not to soften a strong consonant or strengthen a soft one. He must articulate the zayin in ‘you shall remember’ sharply, so that he should not seem to say ‘you shall earn,’ with a sin—that is, so that you should increase reward—for it is not proper to serve the master on condition of receiving a reward.

One who recites in reverse order. He put the third verse before the second and the second before the first, or something similar.

He has not fulfilled his obligation. For it is written, ‘And these words shall be’: they shall remain in their existing order—that is, as they are arranged in the Torah. Nevertheless, if he put the passage ‘And He said’ before the passage ‘And it shall be, if you listen,’ and the passage ‘And it shall be, if you listen’ before ‘Hear,’ it appears that this is not considered reverse order and he has fulfilled his obligation, since they are not arranged one after another in the Torah.

He must return to the place where he made the mistake. If he erred between one section and another, so that he does not know at which section he stopped and to the beginning of which section he should return, he returns to the first break, which is ‘And it shall be, if you listen.’ The Rambam says that it is ‘And you shall love Hashem.’ If he stopped in the middle of a section, knowing the section in which he stopped but not knowing where in that section he stopped, he returns to the beginning of that section. If he was reciting ‘And you shall write them,’ and does not know whether he is at the ‘And you shall write them’ of ‘Hear’ or at the ‘And you shall write them’ of ‘And it shall be, if you listen,’ he returns to the ‘And you shall write them’ of ‘Hear.’ But if the doubt arose after he began ‘So that they may increase,’ he does not return, because he is following the accustomed course of his tongue.

notes.he: בדוגמאות על לבבך, עשב בשדך, ואבדתם מהרה, האות שבסוף המילה הראשונה חוזרת בראש השנייה: ל, ב, מ. תרגום המשמעות לבדו אינו מדגים את חזרת האות.
notes.en: In the examples על לבבך, עשב בשדך, and ואבדתם מהרה, the final letter of the first word recurs at the start of the second: lamed, bais, and mem. Translating the meanings alone does not reproduce this repeated-letter effect.

notes.he: לגבי הספק בין הפרקים מובאות שתי נקודות חזרה שונות: והיה אם שמוע, ולדעת הרמב״ם ואהבת. אין לערב זאת עם הספק באיזו הופעה של וכתבתם עומד הקורא.
notes.en: For uncertainty between sections, two different restart points are given: “And it shall be, if you listen,” and, according to the Rambam, “And you shall love.” This differs from uncertainty about which occurrence of “And you shall write them” the reader has reached.

entries.english:
A course of masonry. A row of stone construction, like ‘courses of large stone’ in Ezra (chapter 6). Although they are afraid lest they fall and cannot concentrate, the Sages did not require them to descend, because the recitation of the Shema requires concentration only in the first verse.

Something they are not permitted to do in the prayer. For prayer is a plea for mercy and requires concentration; therefore they descend below and pray.

notes.he: הכוונה בפסוק הראשון נדרשת גם כאן. אי־הירידה מן האילן או הנדבך אינה ביטול הדרישה, אלא הבחנה בין קריאת שמע לתפילה.
notes.en: Concentration on the first verse is still required here. Not descending from the tree or masonry does not cancel that requirement; it distinguishes the Shema from prayer.

entries.english:
A bridegroom. One who married a virgin is exempt from reciting the Shema on the first night because he is preoccupied lest he not find her to be a virgin. I have heard that he fears lest he become one whose reproductive organ is severed through his intercourse; and this is preoccupation with a commandment. The Merciful One said, ‘And when you walk on the way’: it is in going on your own affairs that you are obliged, but in going on a commandment's affairs you are exempt.

If he has not performed the act. If he has not had intercourse through the night following Shabbos—a period of four nights, he is preoccupied. From then onward he has become familiar with her and is no longer preoccupied; even though he has not performed the act, he is obliged to recite the Shema.

notes.he: מובאים שני הסברים לטרדת החתן: חשש שלא ימצא בתולים, וחשש לפגיעה בגופו בבעילה. ההסבר השני משתמש בביטוי כרות שפכה; משמעותו הגופנית המדויקת כאן אינה ברורה.
notes.en: Two explanations are given for the bridegroom’s preoccupation: fear of not finding virginity, and fear of bodily injury to himself during intercourse. The second uses the expression “one whose reproductive organ is severed”; its precise bodily meaning here is uncertain.

entries.english:
He bathed on the first night after his wife died. Although a mourner is forbidden to bathe.

I am physically delicate. Cold and chilled, an expression of coldness. There would be suffering if he did not bathe, and during his mourning only bathing for pleasure is forbidden.

notes.he: הפירוש משתמש בלשון קור וצינה לביאור אסטניס, ומיד מדגיש את הצער בלי רחיצה. אין הכרח לזהות את הביטוי עם אבחנה רפואית מסוימת.
notes.en: The commentary uses the language of cold and chill to explain physical delicacy and immediately stresses suffering without bathing. The expression need not be identified with a particular medical diagnosis.

entries.english: Not everyone who wishes to take the name upon himself may take it. If he has not been established as wise and abstemious in other matters, [this] is merely pride: he presents himself as able to concentrate his heart. The halacha does not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. We have seen some of our teachers say that nowadays every person should recite the Shema on the first night. Since in these generations people do not concentrate so much on other days, if he does not recite on the first night it looks more like self-importance: he presents himself as concentrating at every other time, and only now not doing so because he is preoccupied with a commandment.

notes.he: הטענה האחרונה הופכת את החשש: כאשר הריכוז בדרך כלל מועט, דווקא ההימנעות בליל החתונה יכולה להיראות כהתרברבות בריכוז הרגיל.
notes.en: The final argument reverses the concern: when concentration is generally limited, refraining on the wedding night can look like boasting about one’s usual concentration.

entries.english:
With what may one kindle? The lamp of Shabbos: from what may one make wicks, and what oils may one use for kindling?

Not with cedar bast. There is a kind of wool in the cedar, between the bark and the wood, called lechesh.

With uncombed flax. Flax that has not been combed.

With silk waste. The waste of silk.

With a wick of willow fiber. There is a kind of wool [in the willow] between the bark and the wood.

With a desert-plant wick. The leaves of a long grass, which people braid and use for kindling.

With the green growth on the surface of the water. A kind of wool that grows on the sides of a ship which has remained in the water for a long time. Up to this point, the disqualification of wicks; from here onward, the disqualification of oils.

Not with pitch or wax. One must not put melted pitch or molten wax in the lamp in place of oil and kindle it. But to make something like a long wick, as people customarily make from wax, is permitted.

Nor with keek oil. Oil that comes from the seeds within cotton, which people call קוטו"ן. Some explain it as the plant of Yonah, a plant with large leaves called כרו"ע in Arabic; the oil that comes from it is exceedingly thick. As for the wicks of which the Sages said that one may not kindle with them, what is the reason? Because the flame flickers around them—that is, the flame does not enter within the wick, [but] goes around it on the outside. As for the oils of which the Sages said that one may not kindle with them, it is because they do not draw along after the wick. Since the lamp does not burn well, we are concerned lest he tilt the oil toward the mouth of the lamp and thereby kindle a fire. Alternatively, lest he leave the lamp and go out; and we hold that the lamp of Shabbos is obligatory.

Nor with oil designated for burning. Oil of the priestly portion that became impure. Why does he call it ‘oil designated for burning’? Since it stands to be burned, for it is forbidden for consumption. We are dealing with a festival that falls on the eve of Shabbos: when he lights the lamp while it is still day, he ends up burning impure oil of the priestly portion on a festival. We hold that consecrated things are not burned on a festival, for it is written (Shemos 12), ‘What remains of it until morning you shall burn in fire.’ We expound the verse thus: What remains of it until the first morning—wait until the second morning and burn it, because the leftover offering is not burned on a festival. The same applies to all other consecrated things that require burning.

But the Sages say: Whether cooked or uncooked, one may not kindle with it. The first teacher also said, ‘Nor with forbidden animal fat,’ which implies all such fat. Rather, there is a difference between the Sages and the first teacher: one of them holds that it is permitted to kindle with cooked forbidden animal fat when any amount of oil is mixed into it, and one forbids it even through a mixture of oil. It was not clarified for the Sages of the Talmud which of the two forbids and which permits. The halacha follows the Sages.

notes.he: לשמן קיק מובאים שני זיהויים: שמן מזרעי כותנה, ושמן מצמח הקיקיון. המילים הזרות קוטו״ן וכרו״ע הן שמות המובאים בפירוש; אין לאחד את שני הצמחים.
notes.en: Two identifications of keek oil are offered: oil from cottonseed and oil from the plant of Yonah. קוטו"ן and כרו"ע are the foreign names quoted in the commentary; the two plants should not be collapsed into one.

notes.he: במחלוקת על תערובת שמן בחלב מבושל לא נתברר מי המתיר ומי האוסר. אין לייחס את ההיתר לחכמים או לתנא קמא בוודאות.
notes.en: In the dispute about oil mixed with cooked forbidden animal fat, it was not established which side permits and which forbids. The permission must not be assigned with certainty to either the Sages or the first teacher.

entries.english:
One may not kindle with oil designated for burning on a festival. He is stating the reason for the preceding Mishna: Why did we learn, ‘Nor with oil designated for burning’? Because one may not kindle with oil designated for burning on a festival, since consecrated things are not burned on a festival.

One may not kindle with tar. The residue of pitch, with an exceedingly bad smell. Nevertheless, it draws along after the wick more readily than pitch because it is soft; therefore, were it not for respect for Shabbos, one could kindle with it.

Sesame. This is its name in Arabic. It is a small, sweet seed, and there is much of it in the Land of Israel.

Radish oil. Oil that comes from radish seed.

Wild gourds. A desert gourd.

Naphtha. It is a kind of pitch, white and foul-smelling. The halacha follows the Sages, that one may kindle with all oils except those disqualified ones enumerated above in the Mishna, and except balsam oil and white naphtha. Each of these two oils flares up and burns, and we are concerned lest he leave it and go out. There is another reason to forbid balsam oil: a decree lest he draw some of it for use because of its value. We hold that one who puts oil into a lamp is liable for kindling, and one who draws some of it for use is liable for extinguishing.

notes.he: נפט מתואר תחילה כלבן, ובהמשך נפט לבן נזכר בין האסורים. שני המשפטים עומדים כאן זה לצד זה; אין להבין מהם היתר גורף לכל נפט.
notes.en: Naphtha is first described as white, but white naphtha is later listed among the prohibited oils. Both statements stand here; they do not establish unrestricted permission for every kind of naphtha.

entries.english:
One may not kindle with anything that comes from a tree. To make a wick from it.

Except flax. It is called ‘tree,’ as it is written (Yehoshua 2), ‘She concealed them in the flax of the tree.’ Even so, one may kindle with a wick made from it. Hemp and cotton are not things that come from a tree, but kinds of seed; therefore one may kindle with them. Flax too is a kind of seed, and it was necessary to include it only because it is called ‘tree,’ as it is written, ‘She concealed them in the flax of the tree.’

Does not contract the impurity of tents. If he made a tent from them and the dead person is beneath it, it is like any other house and does not require sprinkling and immersion, for the tent itself does not receive impurity—only the utensils beneath it do.

Except flax. For the tent itself is impure, as it is written (Bamidbar 19), ‘He shall sprinkle upon the tent.’ We derive ‘tent’ from ‘tent’ in the Tabernacle, of which it is written (Shemos 40), ‘He spread the tent over the Tabernacle.’ In the tent of the Tabernacle there was nothing that comes from a tree except flax, as it is written (there, 26), ‘Ten curtains of twisted linen.’

Which he folded. As people braid wicks.

Singed it. Over the flame, so that it would be scorched and would light well. We are dealing with a piece of cloth measuring exactly three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths.

It is impure. For folding it does not remove its status as a garment, since he has not singed it.

It is pure. For folding it removed its status as a garment, and it is as though it does not contain three by three. Anything smaller than three by three is free of susceptibility to impurity, whether through lesions or through the impurity of a dead person.

And one may not kindle with it. We are dealing with a festival that falls on the eve of Shabbos, when the prohibition of set-aside objects applies. One may not use fragments of utensils broken on that day as fuel, since they have become newly produced objects; but one may use utensils as fuel, since they are fit to be moved. All agree that one who kindles must light most of the portion of the wick protruding outside the lamp before withdrawing his hands. Therefore, the reason Rabbi Eliezer says that one may not kindle with it is that he holds that folding it did not remove its status as a utensil. When he has lit a little of it, since it was exactly three by three, it has become a fragment of a utensil, because less than three by three is not a utensil. When he kindles it by hand to complete most of the protruding portion, he is thus kindling with a fragment of a utensil broken on a festival. For when we say that one may use utensils as fuel, this is specifically provided that he does not touch it after it has diminished. Rabbi Akiva says that one may kindle with it: he holds that folding it removed its status as a utensil from the time he folded it on the eve of the festival, since one may not braid a wick on a festival. Consequently, there is no fragment of a utensil broken on the festival here; therefore one may kindle with it. The halacha follows Rabbi Akiva.

notes.he: השיעור הוא שלוש אצבעות על שלוש בדיוק. לדעת רבי אליעזר תחילת השרפה מפחיתה אותו משיעור כלי; לדעת רבי עקיבא כבר בטל שם כלי בקיפול מערב יום טוב.
notes.en: The cloth is exactly three fingerbreadths by three. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the start of burning reduces it below the size of a utensil; according to Rabbi Akiva, folding before the festival had already removed that status.

notes.he: טהורה היא מבאר את מעמד הבגד בדיני טומאה, ואילו ההסבר על הדלקה עוסק בדיני יום טוב. אלה שני עניינים נפרדים במחלוקת רבי אליעזר ורבי עקיבא.
notes.en: “It is pure” explains the cloth’s ritual status, while the discussion of kindling concerns festival law. These are distinct questions in the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva.

entries.english:
An eggshell. The hard outer shell within which the egg lies.

So that it drips. Drop by drop into the lamp. The reason is a decree lest he draw some of it for use; since he designated it for the lamp, he is liable for extinguishing.

Even if it is made of earthenware. Which is repulsive. Even so, we impose the decree: since the burning wick is not within the vessel containing the oil, he may come to draw some of it for use, thinking that there is no extinguishing here.

Rabbi Yehudah permits it. He does not decree lest he come to draw some of it for use, for he sees the oil dripping onto the wick beneath it.

If the potter joined it from the outset, etc. The same applies if the householder joined it with lime or potters' clay on the eve of Shabbos: there is no cause for concern, for because of the prohibition of Shabbos he keeps away from it.

And put the end of the wick. The end that extends from the side, to draw up the oil; it is drawn along the wick to the burning end. The Mishna teaches us the dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages concerning an eggshell, an earthenware vessel, and a bowl. Had it taught us only the eggshell, we might have thought that it is in this case that the Sages speak: since it is not repulsive, he may come to draw some of it for use; but with earthenware, which is repulsive, one might say that they agree with Rabbi Yehudah. Had it taught us earthenware, we might have thought that it is in this case that Rabbi Yehudah speaks, but in that other case he agrees with the Sages. Had it taught us only these two, we might have thought that it is in these cases that Rabbi Yehudah speaks, because the eggshell and the earthenware vessel rest above, within the hollow of the lamp, with nothing intervening between the lamp and them. There is no reason to decree lest he draw some for use, because he keeps away from it. But with a bowl, which is separate—for it rests beside the lamp, and there is a separation here, and one cannot say that it is the lamp itself—one might say that he agrees that we should decree. Had it taught us that case, we might have thought that it is in that case that the Sages speak, but in these other two they agree with Rabbi Yehudah. All are necessary. The halacha follows the Sages.

notes.he: הפירוש מצריך שלוש דוגמאות: קליפת ביצה שאינה מאוסה, כלי חרס מאוס, וקערה נפרדת. בכל שלב נבחנת אפשרות אחרת להגביל את המחלוקת.
notes.en: The commentary requires three examples: an eggshell that is not repulsive, a repulsive earthenware vessel, and a separate bowl. Each stage tests a different possible limitation of the dispute.

entries.english:
Because of idolaters. Such as Persians who do not permit a light to be kindled on their festival day except in their house of idolatrous worship.

Because of robbers. So that they should not see that a person is there and come upon him.

Because of an evil spirit. Which rests upon him, and when he does not see, he is at ease. The Rambam explained ‘an evil spirit’ as one of the kinds of illness that come upon those afflicted by black bile: they find rest only when they sit in darkness and hidden from people.

Or so that the sick person may sleep, he is exempt. This sick person is one whose condition involves danger. If he extinguishes for a sick person whose condition does not involve danger, he is liable according to this teacher's view, that one is liable for labor not needed for its own sake. Likewise, the cases of idolaters, robbers, and an evil spirit all involve danger. Strictly speaking, he should have taught ‘permitted’; but because he wished to teach ‘liable’ in the latter clause, he taught ‘exempt’ in the first clause.

To spare the wick, he is liable. Even though he does not need the extinguishing itself, but needs something else—that the wick should not burn away or the lamp crack—he is liable, because one is liable for labor not needed for its own sake.

He exempts in all these cases except that of the wick. For the only extinguishing that is needed for its own sake is the extinguishing of coals and the extinguishing involved in singeing a wick, where he extinguishes in order to make the flame take hold quickly when he wishes to light it. The halacha does not follow Rabbi Yoasai.

Because he makes it into charcoal. He intends now, through this extinguishing, to make it into charcoal, so that it will be singed and give a good light.

notes.he: במשנה כתוב גוים, ואילו לשון הדיבור בפירוש היא עובדי כוכבים. הדוגמה בפירוש היא איסור הדלקה בחג הפרסים מחוץ לבית עבודתם.
notes.en: The Mishna says “gentiles,” while the commentary’s lemma says “idolaters.” The example in the commentary concerns a Persian festival restriction on kindling outside their place of worship.

notes.he: מובאות לשון רוח רעה ופרשנות הרמב״ם על חולי של מרה שחורה. אלה מונחים של התיאור הקדום, ולא זיהוי ודאי של מחלה מודרנית.
notes.en: Both the expression “evil spirit” and the Rambam’s explanation involving an illness of black bile are given. These are terms of the older account, not a certain identification of a modern illness.

notes.he: ההיתר ברישא מוסבר מצד סכנה. הביטוי מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה מתייחס לפעולה שאינה נחוצה לתכליתה העצמית, ולא למעשה בלי כוונה כלל.
notes.en: The opening permission is explained by danger. “Labor not needed for its own sake” means an act not required for its own intrinsic purpose, not an entirely unintentional act.

entries.english:
At the time of childbirth. At a time of danger, punishment is at hand.

And the dough portion and kindling the lamp. Because these are the needs of the household and she is regularly in the house, they depend upon her.

notes.he: הפירוש קושר פורענות לשעת סכנה. זהו הסבר מוסרי כללי; אין בו קביעה על חטאיה של יולדת מסוימת.
notes.en: The commentary connects punishment with a time of danger. This is a general moral explanation, not a determination of the sins of any particular woman in childbirth.

entries.english:
A person must say within his household. He must say these things gently, so that they will accept them from him.

As darkness approaches. When it is close to darkness and there is still time left in the day to tithe and to make joining arrangements. But not long before darkness, lest they be negligent and say, ‘There is still time left in the day.’

Have you tithed? For the Shabbos meal, since even casual eating on Shabbos establishes an obligation to tithe.

Have you made the joining arrangements? The joining arrangements for travel limits and courtyards. These two are suitably stated as questions, since perhaps they have already done them. But concerning the lamp it is not suitable to say, ‘Have you kindled the lamp?’ because whether it has been kindled or not is something visible to the eye.

If it is doubtful whether darkness has fallen. From the beginning of sunset, as long as only one star is visible, it is definitely day. As long as two medium-sized stars are visible, it is doubtful whether darkness has fallen, and this is called twilight; we impose upon it the stringencies of day and the stringencies of night. Once three medium-sized stars are visible, it is definitely night in every respect.

One may not tithe produce that is definitely untithed. For this is a full act of making it fit. Although it is forbidden only as a rabbinic restriction, this teacher holds that they imposed the rabbinic restriction even at twilight.

And one may not immerse vessels. To remove them from their impurity, for it is like repairing a utensil, and this too involves a rabbinic restriction.

And one may not kindle the lamps. All the more so, because this is a matter of doubt concerning a Torah prohibition; he is teaching ‘this, and it need not be said that.’ My teachers explained ‘And one may not kindle the lamps’ as: One may not tell a gentile to kindle them.

But one may tithe doubtfully tithed produce. This is not like making something fit, because most unlearned people do tithe.

And make joining arrangements. Joining arrangements for courtyards, which are merely a stringency, but not joining arrangements for travel limits, which have support from Scriptural verses.

And insulate hot food. In something that does not add heat; for with something that adds heat it is forbidden even while it is still day. The reason one may insulate hot food at twilight in something that does not add heat is that insulating hot food on Shabbos itself in something that does not add heat was forbidden only as a decree lest he find that his pot has cooled and bring it to the boil over the fire, thereby cooking on Shabbos. At twilight there is no reason to decree on this account, because ordinary pots are boiling hot at twilight, and there is no concern lest it have cooled and he bring it to the boil. Therefore one may insulate hot food at twilight, although one may not insulate it on Shabbos.

notes.he: מספר הכוכבים וגודלם הם חלק מן ההבחנה שבפירוש. אין להפוך תיאור זה ללוח זמנים אחיד לכל מקום בלי בירור הלכתי של שקיעה וצאת הכוכבים.
notes.en: The number and size of stars form part of the commentary’s distinction. This description should not be converted into a uniform timetable for every place without determining the laws of sunset and nightfall.

notes.he: היתר ההטמנה כאן הוא בבין השמשות ובחומר שאינו מוסיף חום. חומר המוסיף חום אסור גם מבעוד יום, ואילו ההטמנה בשבת עצמה נאסרת כאן מטעם החשש לחימום מחדש.
notes.en: The permission here is at twilight and with material that does not add heat. Heat-adding material is forbidden even before night; insulation on Shabbos itself is prohibited here because of the concern for reheating.

entries.english:
How does the case of a brother's wife, etc., arise? She exempts her co-wife.

Another brother was born to them. He found her already bound to a surviving brother for levirate marriage, while she was forbidden to him as the wife of a brother who had not shared his lifetime.

The second brother then took his brother's wife in levirate marriage. He also had another wife.

And died. Without children.

The first woman. She is the first brother's wife, who had already once fallen for levirate marriage. She leaves without a levirate obligation as the wife of a brother who had not shared his lifetime.

He made with her. The brother who died did so.

A preliminary levirate betrothal. This means that he betrothed her with money. For a woman awaiting levirate marriage, betrothal with money is not a complete betrothal; its force is only rabbinic. She is not acquired by the surviving brother as a fully married woman until he has intercourse with her, and this brother died before he managed to take her into marriage.

The second woman receives levirate release. She is not exempt as the co-wife of a forbidden relative, because she is not fully her co-wife.

But may not enter levirate marriage. Since preliminary betrothal effects a partial acquisition, she is partly the co-wife of a forbidden relative. Wherever the betrothal is incomplete, she receives levirate release but may not enter levirate marriage.

notes.he: מאמר בכסף יוצר קניין חלקי מדרבנן, ולא נישואין גמורים. לכן האשה האחרת אינה נפטרת כצרת ערוה גמורה, אבל גם אינה מתייבמת.
notes.en: Monetary preliminary betrothal creates only a partial rabbinic acquisition, not full marriage. The other wife is therefore neither wholly exempt as a forbidden relative’s co-wife nor available for levirate marriage.

notes.he: הנפילה הקודמת היתה מן האח הראשון אל האח השני. המיתה שבסוף המקרה היא מיתת האח השני בלא ילדים; אין להחליף בין שני האחים המתים.
notes.en: The earlier levirate succession was from the first brother to the second. The death at the end is the second brother’s childless death; the two deceased brothers must not be confused.

entries.english:
And died. The brother who had performed levirate marriage.

He may marry whichever he chooses by levirate marriage. She thereby exempts the other woman. This does not refer to the clause about preliminary betrothal, but to the opening case, where the first woman was said to be forbidden, etc. Rabbi Shimon says that, since she had already entered levirate marriage when the youngest brother was born, she had never been bound to this brother through her marriage to the first brother, and is permitted to him. The law does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

notes.he: היתר רבי שמעון מנומק בכך שהאח הצעיר נולד כשהאשה כבר היתה נשואה לאח השני. הפירוש שולל במפורש את החלת דבריו על מאמר בלבד, ואינו פוסק כמותו.
notes.en: Rabbi Shimon’s permission depends on the youngest brother being born after the woman had already married the second brother. The commentary explicitly excludes the preliminary-betrothal-only clause and does not rule in his favor.

entries.english:
She neither receives levirate release nor enters levirate marriage. Her co-wife is meant, and all the more so the woman herself. The same applies to a woman classified as אַיְלוֹנִית, since Scripture says, 'Whom she will bear' (Devarim 25), excluding such a woman. Likewise the wife of a congenital eunuch or of a person classified as אַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס neither receives levirate release nor enters levirate marriage, for it says, 'And he has no son' (ibid.), excluding those not capable of having children. The wife of a convert and the wife of a freed slave likewise neither receive levirate release nor enter levirate marriage, since converts and slaves do not have the brotherhood relevant here. But an infertile woman and an elderly woman may either receive levirate release or enter levirate marriage.

Her sister. The sister of the forbidden relative.

When she is her fellow widow awaiting levirate marriage. For example, two sisters fall to him from two of his brothers, and one is forbidden to him as a close relative, such as his mother-in-law or daughter-in-law.

She receives levirate release or enters levirate marriage. He is not then encountering the sister of a woman bound to him, because the forbidden relative is not bound to him for levirate marriage.

notes.he: איילונית ועקרה אינן שמות חלופיים כאן: הראשונה נמנית בפטורות והשנייה בחולצות או מתייבמות. סריס חמה ואנדרוגינוס הם סיווגים הלכתיים במקור; אין לזהות אותם כאן עם אבחנה רפואית בת זמננו.
notes.en: The categories אַיְלוֹנִית and an infertile woman are not interchangeable here: the former is exempt, while the latter may receive release or enter levirate marriage. Congenital eunuch and אַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס are the source’s legal classifications; no modern medical diagnosis is being assigned.

notes.he: היתר האחות נובע מכך שהערוה אינה זקוקה לו כלל. אין להחילו על כל שתי אחיות שנפלו לפניו כששתיהן זקוקות.
notes.en: The sister is permitted because the forbidden relative has no levirate bond to him at all. This is not a permission for any pair of sisters where both are bound to him.

entries.english:
Secondary relatives. Relatives whose prohibition was decreed by the Sages in addition to the primary forbidden relationships. These are called a commandment prohibition, because it is a commandment to obey the Sages. They are: his mother's mother, with no upper generational limit; only his mother's father's mother; his father's mother, with no upper generational limit; [and his father's father's mother]; his father's father's wife, with no upper generational limit; only his mother's father's wife; the wife of his father's brother related through their mother; the wife of his mother's brother related either through their mother or through their father; his son's daughter-in-law, with no further generational limit; his daughter's daughter-in-law; his son's daughter's daughter; his daughter's daughter's daughter; his son's son's daughter; his daughter's son's daughter; his wife's son's daughter's daughter; his wife's daughter's daughter's daughter; his wife's father's mother's mother; his wife's mother's mother's mother; his wife's mother's father's mother; and his wife's father's father's mother.

A widow in relation to a High Priest. His brother, an ordinary priest, died, and that brother's wife fell to him for levirate marriage.

A divorced woman or a woman released from levirate marriage in relation to an ordinary priest. For example, his deceased brother had transgressed by marrying a divorced woman or a woman released from levirate marriage. When the brother dies, she requires levirate release, because his betrothal of her had legal effect: betrothal takes effect in relationships forbidden by a negative commandment. But levirate marriage is not allowed, since she is forbidden to him. Nor can she be exempted without any act, because a negative commandment is not strong enough to exempt her: the exemption is learned from a wife's sister, whose prohibition carries excision.

notes.he: ״אין לה הפסק״ באם אמו מתייחס לשרשרת אמהות מעל אם אמו, ובאם אביו לשרשרת אמהות מעל אם אביו. באשת אבי אביו מדובר בנשות האבות שבקו האבהי, ובכלת בנו בנשות הבנים שבקו היורד; אין זו הרחבה לכל ענף משפחתי.
notes.en: For his mother’s mother, no limit follows the maternal chain above that grandmother; for his father’s mother, it follows the maternal chain above that grandmother. For his father’s father’s wife it follows wives of paternal ancestors; for his son’s daughter-in-law it follows wives along the descending male line. It does not extend every branch indiscriminately.

notes.he: המקור מונה בסוגריים את ״ואם אבי אביו״, אחרי אם אביו שאין לה הפסק. זהו יחס משפחתי נפרד משרשרת האימהות שמעל אם אביו; היקפו של הפריט המוסגר בתוך הרשימה טעון בירור.
notes.en: The source lists “and his father’s father’s mother” in brackets after his father’s mother, whose maternal chain has no upper limit. This is a different family branch from the maternal chain above his father’s mother; the scope of the bracketed item within the list remains uncertain.

notes.he: הדוגמה היא נישואין אסורים שהיו תקפים, ולכן לאחר מיתת הבעל אין היתר להינשא בלא חליצה. חיוב החליצה אינו היתר לייבם.
notes.en: The example is a prohibited but legally effective marriage. After the husband dies, its effect prevents the widow from marrying freely without release. Requiring release does not permit levirate marriage.

entries.english:
A brother of any status. Even a mamzer.

His brother in every respect. For inheriting him and becoming ritually impure for his burial.

A slave woman or a non-Jewish woman. Her child's status follows hers. Concerning a slave woman it is written, 'The woman and her children shall belong to her master' (Shemos 21). Concerning a non-Jewish woman it is written, 'For he will turn your son away from following Me' (Devarim 7). Since Scripture does not say, 'For she will turn away,' learn that it means: Do not give your daughter to his son, for your daughter's husband will turn your son, whom your daughter bears to him, away from following Me. It does not refer back to, 'Do not take his daughter for your son,' because the son born from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son, but her son.

notes.he: הדרשה מבחינה בין ״יסיר״ בלשון זכר ובין ״תסיר״ בלשון נקבה. ״בנך״ מוסב בפירוש על בן בתך, ואילו בן הנכרית נקרא כאן בנה.
notes.en: The interpretation turns on the masculine “he will turn away,” rather than the feminine “she will turn away.” “Your son” is explained as your daughter’s son; the child of the non-Jewish woman is called her son here.

entries.english:
He does not know which one he betrothed. Both are forbidden to him, since either may be his wife's sister.

He gives levirate release to both. He does not know which is his brother's widow. He cannot give release to one and take the other in levirate marriage, since she is the sister of the woman he released and is forbidden to him by rabbinic law during that woman's lifetime. Nor may he first enter levirate marriage: perhaps she is not his brother's widow, and he would encounter the sister of the woman bound to him, who is treated like his wife.

If he had two brothers, one gives levirate release. First to one woman. The second brother may then, if he wishes, marry the other by levirate marriage. If she is his brother's widow, this is proper; if she is that widow's sister, he has not encountered the sister of a woman bound to him, because the first woman's release has dissolved the bond.

They went ahead and married. Before consulting the court.

The women are not removed from their marriages. Each man can say, 'My marriage was proper.' Even if the facts were reversed, and the first to marry had married the sister of the woman bound to him, he committed the prohibition at that time; once his brother came and married the second woman, who was the actual brother's widow, her bond to the other brother was dissolved retroactively.

notes.he: החליצה חייבת לבוא תחילה. לאחריה יכול האח השני לשאת את האשה האחרת, אבל אם איננה אלמנת אחיו זו אישות רגילה ולא ייבום.
notes.en: Release must come first. The second brother may then marry the other woman; if she is not his brother’s widow, this is an ordinary marriage rather than levirate marriage.

notes.he: הפקעת הזיקה למפרע אינה מוחקת את האיסור שנעשה בשעת הכניסה הראשונה. הפירוש מסביר מדוע אין מפרידים לאחר מעשה, ואינו מתיר לדלג לכתחילה על החליצה.
notes.en: Retroactive dissolution of the bond does not erase the prohibition committed at the first marriage. The commentary explains nonseparation after the event, not an initial right to omit release.

entries.english:
Two men betrothed two sisters. The men are unrelated to one another.

Each gives levirate release to both, etc. Each is forbidden to enter levirate marriage, because either might encounter the sister of the woman bound to him.

The lone brother gives levirate release to both. He cannot marry either woman by levirate marriage: not before release of the other, because of the sister of a woman bound to him; and not after release, because of the sister of a woman he released. Since he cannot enter levirate marriage, he must therefore first release both, so that the woman who is actually his brother's widow is freed from the prohibition against marrying an outsider before levirate release.

Of the two brothers, one gives levirate release. To dissolve the bond to his brother if this woman is their brother's widow, making her sister permissible to the second brother either way. If the second woman is his brother's widow, it is proper; if she is that widow's sister, the widow's bond to him has already been dissolved by his brother's release.

A brother of this man marries the woman released by the other family. Either way, his marriage is proper. If she is his brother's widow, his brother did not release her, but her sister, who was not their brother's widow, so that release has no effect. If she is not his brother's widow, the marriage is still proper: she is unrelated to him. There is no prohibition of a bound widow's sister, because his brother released her sister, who is their actual brother's widow, dissolving the bond. Nor is she a widow forbidden to marry an outsider before release, because she has received release from her husband's brother.

Two brothers went ahead. Two brothers of one deceased man gave release to both women, because they did not know which was their brother's widow.

They must not enter levirate marriage. The other two brothers must not each marry one woman, because the first to marry might be marrying the sister of the woman bound to him.

Rather, one gives levirate release. First, to one woman.

And one enters levirate marriage. With the second woman. Either way this is proper: if she is his brother's widow, well and good; if not, he has not encountered a bound widow's sister, since his brother has released their brother's widow. Nor is she a widow forbidden to an outsider before release, since she has received release from her husband's brother.

If they went ahead. These last two married after the other two brothers had given release, without coming to consult the court. The women are not removed from their marriages, as explained above. The first marriage involves only a possible prohibition of a bound widow's sister. It may be that the first man married his actual brother's widow properly, and the second also properly married an unrelated woman. Even if the marriages were reversed and the first man encountered a bound widow's sister, once the second brother entered levirate marriage, her bond to his brother was dissolved and that brother's wife became permitted to him. The prohibition he committed remains a past act.

notes.he: חליצה של משפחה אחת אינה מחליפה חליצה של המשפחה האחרת. אם האשה שהוא נושא היא אלמנת אחיו, אחיו חלץ קודם לאחותה, שאינה אלמנת אחיהם, וחליצתו אינה כלום; נישואיו לאלמנת אחיו הם ייבום. אם אינה אלמנת אחיו, אחיו חלץ לאחותה שהיא אלמנת אחיהם, והיא עצמה קיבלה חליצה מאחי בעלה שבמשפחה האחרת; נישואיו עמה הם נישואין רגילים.
notes.en: One family’s release does not substitute for the other family’s release. If the woman he marries is his brother’s actual widow, his own brother’s earlier release was given to her sister, who was not their brother’s widow, and has no effect; his marriage is levirate marriage. If she is not his brother’s widow, his brother has released her sister, the actual widow, and she herself has received release from her own husband’s brother in the other family; his marriage to her is ordinary marriage.

notes.he: גם כאן שני האחים האחרונים כנסו רק אחרי חליצת שני האחים מן המשפחה האחרת. ״ואיסורא דעבד עבד״ מטעים שהמעשה האסור נשאר מעשה שנעשה; אין כאן אישור להקדימו.
notes.en: Here too the final pair married only after the two brothers of the other family had given release. The closing phrase treats the prohibition as a past violation; it does not authorize committing it first.

entries.english:
The duty is for the eldest to enter levirate marriage. For we interpret, 'He shall take her as his wife and perform levirate marriage with her; and the firstborn shall be': the brother who marries her is to be the eldest. 'Whom she will bear': that widow must be capable of bearing, excluding a woman classified as אַיְלוֹנִית. 'The firstborn shall succeed': the brother performing levirate marriage succeeds in his brother's name by inheriting him, and the other brothers do not share with him.

The man accused concerning a married woman. Suspected of relations with a married woman.

They removed her. The court removed her from her husband's marriage because this man had made her forbidden to her husband; this man then went and married her.

He must divorce her. By Torah law she is forbidden to him as she is to her husband. We interpret the repetition of 'was defiled' twice as one prohibition for the husband and one for the man who had relations with her. This applies specifically to someone accused concerning a married woman. Concerning one accused of relations with an unmarried woman, however, it appears that marrying her is a commandment, as we find concerning a rapist: 'She shall be his wife' (Devarim 22).

notes.he: הפירוש מביא את דין האונס כמקור לטענתו על נישואי פנויה, ולא כקביעה שכל חשד יוצר חיוב נישואין. אין ללמוד מכאן היתר לפגיעה או כפייה, או פסק מעשי בלא בירור תנאי הדין.
notes.en: The commentary cites the law concerning a rapist as support for its claim about an unmarried woman, not as a rule that every accusation creates a marriage duty. This does not authorize assault or coercion, nor supply a practical ruling without the law’s conditions.

entries.english:
One who brings a bill of divorce from overseas. He must say, 'It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.' The reason is explained in Gittin: according to one opinion, because they are not expert in the requirement that it be written specifically for this woman; according to another, because witnesses are not readily available to authenticate it.

He must not marry the man's wife. Because we rely upon his declaration.

He died; I killed him, etc. Since her remarriage rests upon his testimony, people could speak disparagingly: perhaps he desired her and gave false testimony about her. She may, however, marry someone else, for a woman may remarry on the evidence of a single witness.

Rabbi Yehudah says: If he says, 'I killed him,' the wife may not remarry. Not even someone else on the strength of this testimony, since he is wicked, and the Torah says not to appoint a wicked man as a witness. The law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah: we hold that a person cannot establish himself as wicked by his own statement, because a person is considered related to himself. We believe him that the man was killed, but do not believe the part of his statement claiming that he himself killed him. Consequently, even if he says, 'I killed him,' the wife may remarry.

If he says, 'We killed him,' the wife may remarry. The Gemara explains that he means, 'I was with those who killed him, but I did not kill him.'

notes.he: מקבלים כאן את הידיעה שהבעל נהרג בלי לקבל את הודאת העד שהרג בעצמו. ההיתר הוא להינשא לאחר; איסור נישואיה לעד שבמשנה אינו מתבטל.
notes.en: The fact that the husband was killed is accepted without accepting the witness’s admission that he personally killed him. Permission is to marry another man; the Mishna’s ban on marrying the witness remains.

entries.english:
Through a vow. She vowed not to benefit from her husband, he did not annul her vow, and she came to a sage for its release. He found no opening for regret.

He must not marry her. Because of suspicion.

Because he is a court. That is, this sage did not conduct repudiation of a marriage or levirate release alone. For we hold that levirate release and repudiations involve two and three, who are not suspected. Release of vows, by contrast, can be done by a single expert.

All of them. The sage, the messenger bringing the divorce document, and the witness testifying so that a woman may remarry, of whom we learned that they must not marry her. If they had wives at the time of the event and those wives subsequently died, the women may marry them, since suspicion no longer applies.

All of them. These women.

Who married others. After the sage prohibited her to her husband or the witness testified that her husband had died, and the second husbands then died.

May marry. The sage, the witness, or the messenger who brought the divorce document.

All may marry their sons or their brothers. The sons and brothers of the men whose actions permit the women to remarry. The women are forbidden only to the men themselves, since a person does not sin for the sake of his son or his brother. In all these cases where we say he must not marry her, if he did marry her, he need not divorce her, except for the man accused concerning a married woman. If the court removed her from her husband's marriage on witnesses and clear proof, even if he married her, he must divorce her. If witnesses came only to an indecent circumstance, such as seeing a man leave while she was fastening an apron, or seeing a man leave while she was standing up from the bed, or the like, he need not divorce her if he married her. If, after witnesses to an indecent circumstance came, an unceasing report spread and persisted for a day and a half, he must divorce her if he married her, unless he had children by her: then he does not divorce her, so as not to cast aspersions on his children.

notes.he: ״בשנים ושלשה״ אינו מחלק במפורש את המספרים בין מיאון לחליצה. הטענה כאן היא שהחכם לא פעל לבדו; אין להסיק מן הלשון לבדה הרכב בית דין למעשה.
notes.en: “Two and three” does not explicitly allocate the numbers between repudiation and levirate release. The argument is that the sage did not act alone; this wording alone does not determine a practical court composition.

notes.he: הפירוש מפריד בין עדים וראיה ברורה, עדי דבר מכוער בלבד, וקול שאינו פוסק יום וחצי אחרי העדים. אין להחליף את שלושת מסלולי הראיה בחשד סתמי. חריג הבנים נאמר במסלול הקול, ולא כהיתר ראשוני לשאת אשת איש.
notes.en: The commentary separates witnesses with clear proof, witnesses only to an indecent circumstance, and an uninterrupted day-and-a-half report after those witnesses. These three evidentiary branches are not mere unspecified suspicion. The children exception is stated in the persistent-report branch, not as initial permission to marry a married woman.

entries.english:
In what way is the foot an established source of damage? That is, in which matter is the foot regarded as prone? The answer is: to break things in the course of walking. This is what it is prone to do: break vessels while walking.

The animal is considered prone. The opening clause taught primary categories: actual foot damage, where the animal trod with its feet. The later clause taught derivative categories: an animal is prone to walk normally and break things with its body, its hair, or the pack upon it as it walks.

If it was kicking. This is abnormal conduct and a derivative of horn. Therefore liability is half damages and no more.

Or pebbles were flying out. Although this is not abnormal conduct but the animal's usual behavior, liability is nevertheless half damages and no more, because this is a received legal tradition. The case is in the injured party's domain: in the public domain the owner is exempt, for pebble damage is a derivative of foot, carrying foot's exemption in the public domain.

It fell on another vessel. Damage to the first is foot damage, for which full damages are paid; the last was broken through the mechanism of pebble damage, so liability is half damages.

An object was tied to its foot. Anything tied to a fowl's foot is called a dileel. Some texts read dilee.

Hopping about. Dancing. Some explain it as digging in the ground with its feet, as fowl do.

The owner pays half damages. The tied object is treated as pebble damage: with that object the bird sent pebbles onto the vessels. Hopping about likewise refers to a case where the bird propelled pebbles and those pebbles broke the vessels.

notes.he: צרורות הם תולדת רגל לענין פטור ברשות הרבים, אף שחיובם ברשות הניזק חצי נזק. בעיטה, לעומת זאת, היא שינוי ותולדת קרן.
notes.en: Pebble damage is a derivative of foot for the public-domain exemption, even though its liability in the injured party’s domain is half damages. Kicking, by contrast, is abnormal and belongs to horn.

notes.he: ״דליל״ מוגדר ככל דבר הקשור ברגל התרנגולת; גרסת ״דלי״ נמסרת כחלופה. אין לזהות מן המלה לבדה חפץ מסוים או לשנות את סוג הנזק.
notes.en: The term dileel is defined as anything tied to a fowl’s foot; dilee is recorded as an alternative reading. The word alone does not identify a particular object or change the damage category.

entries.english:
In what way is the tooth an established source of damage? In which matter is it regarded as prone? The answer is: to eat what is appropriate for it.

The owner pays half damages. Because this is abnormal conduct.

Where does this apply, etc.? This refers to eating fruit or vegetables. In the public domain the owner is exempt, since we require, 'It grazed in another's field.' But if it ate clothing or utensils, even in the public domain the owner owes half damages. People do put clothing and utensils in the public domain temporarily; this is therefore horn damage in the public domain, for which the owner is liable.

The owner pays for the benefit received. This is not full compensation. If the animal ate something expensive, it is valued as though it were barley, and the owner pays only the discounted price of barley, one third below its market selling price. If it ate something worth less than barley, the owner pays the discounted value of what it ate. If it ate something that harmed it, such as wheat, the owner is exempt, since it received no benefit.

From the sides of the square, the owner pays for the damage. If the animal went and stood at the sides of the square, where oxen do not normally walk, that place is not treated as the public domain, and the damage is paid for.

notes.he: בהערכת ההנאה, מאכל יקר מוערך כשעורים בזול: שליש פחות ממחיר השוק, לא שליש ממחיר השוק. מאכל הזול משעורים מוערך לפי ערכו שלו בזול; מאכל שהזיק לה אינו הנאה.
notes.en: For benefit, expensive food is valued as discounted barley: one third below market price, not one third of market price. Food cheaper than barley uses its own discounted value; harmful food supplies no benefit.

entries.english:
Because they are considered prone. To jump. This is in the injured party's domain, since it is a derivative of foot.

A cake baked on coals. A cake that is baked upon coals.

For the cake, full damages are paid. This is tooth damage in the injured party's domain.

For the stack, half damages are paid. It is like pebble damage, for which we have a received legal tradition that half damages are paid.

notes.he: הדין על הגדיש נלמד כאן מדין צרורות. אין להסיק שכל נזק אש של כלב מוגבל לחצי בלי תנאי המקרה של החררה והגדיש.
notes.en: The stack is treated here by the law of pebble damage. This does not establish a half-damages ceiling for every fire caused by a dog, independently of this cake-and-stack case.

entries.english:
After it refrains for three days. It sees oxen and does not gore; it then returns to its status of not being established as prone to gore.

Three occasions. Even within one day. The law does not follow Rabbi [Meir]: it is not established as prone to gore until testimony concerns three days.

They handle it. They pull it and play with it, and it does not gore. In this matter the law follows [Rabbi Meir]: an ox established as prone to gore does not return to its former status until children play with it.

notes.he: הסוגריים ״מאיר״ הם מן המקור. בפסק זה אין הלכה כרבי מאיר: דרושים שלושה ימים להיעשות מועד. בפסק הבא המקור פוסק כמותו בחזרה לתמות; אין סתירה בין שתי ההכרעות.
notes.en: The brackets around Meir belong to the source. This ruling rejects Rabbi Meir’s test for becoming established: three days are required. The next ruling follows him for returning to the former status, so the two decisions do not conflict.

notes.he: גם ״כרבי מאיר״ נתון בסוגריים במקור. כאן ילדים מושכים ומשחקים בשור והוא אינו נוגח; אין זו אותה בדיקה של שלוש פעמים שבה דן הקטע הקודם.
notes.en: The source also brackets the words identifying Rabbi Meir here. Children pull and play with the ox and it does not gore; this is a different test from the preceding three-occasions question.

entries.english:
It gored, pushed with its body, etc. All are derivatives of horn.

It is enough for what is inferred to be like its source case. You infer horn damage in the injured party's domain from horn damage in the public domain, saying: Since horn is treated strictly in the public domain, should it not be treated strictly in the injured party's domain? It is enough for the inferred case to be like its source, horn in the public domain. Liability in the injured party's domain must therefore be only half damages, just as it is in the public domain.

I do not infer horn from horn. As we said above; rather, horn from foot. Where the law is strict with tooth and foot, should it not be strict with horn?

It is enough for what is inferred by the argument. Ultimately, without horn in the public domain you cannot find a basis for the argument from lesser to greater. Rabbi Tarfon does accept the limiting principle elsewhere, since it is a Torah rule. Scripture says, 'Would she not be shamed for seven days?' (Bamidbar 12). An argument from lesser to greater would yield fourteen days for the Divine Presence, but it is enough for the inferred case to be like its source. Therefore she is shut away for seven days and no more. Nevertheless, he does not accept the limiting principle here. Rabbi Tarfon holds that we apply it where it does not completely undo the inference. In that case, seven days for the Divine Presence are not written explicitly. The inference introduces fourteen; the limiting principle removes seven and leaves seven. The inference has thus established those remaining seven days and has not been completely undone. Here, however, half damages are written for both the public domain and the injured party's courtyard. The inference introduces another half, making full damages. If you apply the limiting principle and leave only half damages as before, the inference is undone and achieves nothing at all. The Sages hold that we apply the limiting principle even where it completely undoes the inference. The law follows the Sages.

notes.he: רבי טרפון מקבל בדרך כלל ״דיו״, אבל אינו מפעילו כשהוא מבטל את כל תוספת הקל וחומר. חכמים מפעילים אותו גם אז. ארבעה עשר הימים בדוגמת מרים הם תוצאת הקל וחומר הנדחית, לא משך הסגר שנפסק.
notes.en: Rabbi Tarfon generally accepts the limiting principle, but not where it cancels the inference’s entire addition. The Sages apply it even there. The fourteen days in the Miriam example are the inference’s rejected result, not the decided period of confinement.

entries.english:
Whether awake or asleep. If one person was sleeping and another came and lay down to sleep beside him, the second is liable if he injures the first; the first is exempt if he injures the second. If they lay down together, whichever injures the other is liable, since each is regarded as an established source of damage in relation to the other.

He blinded another's eye. Even inadvertently, he owes damages, but not the four other payments. Liability for the four other payments arises only from deliberate conduct or conduct close to deliberate.

notes.he: מי ששכב אחר כך נושא באחריות כלפי הישן הראשון; הראשון פטור בנזק לשני. אם שכבו יחד האחריות הדדית.
notes.en: The later sleeper bears liability toward the first; the first is exempt for injuring the later arrival. If they lay down together, liability is mutual.

notes.he: הנזק הוא תשלום אחד; ״ארבעה דברים״ הם ארבעה תשלומים אחרים. הפירוש דורש מזיד או קרוב למזיד להם, ולא מחיל אותם אוטומטית על שוגג.
notes.en: Damages are one payment; the “four things” are four other payments. The commentary requires deliberate or near-deliberate conduct for them, rather than imposing them automatically for inadvertent harm.

entries.english: Any sacrifices whose blood was received by a non-priest. Someone who is not a priest: the sacrifice is invalid. For it is written (Vayikra 22), 'They shall keep apart from the holy offerings of the children of Israel and shall not profane them.' This teaches that a non-priest who performed the service profaned the sacred offerings. A mourner on the day of death. Someone whose relative has died, from among those for whom he is obliged to mourn, is called a first-day mourner throughout the day of the death and is forbidden to eat sacred offerings. If he performed the service, he profaned it. The exception is the High Priest, who offers sacrifices while in this state of mourning. One who has immersed but awaits sunset. His purification is not complete until his sun has set, as it is written (ibid.), 'The sun shall set, and he shall be pure.' One lacking the required garments. An ordinary priest who served in fewer than four garments, or a High Priest who served in fewer than eight. Just as someone lacking garments is disqualified, so is someone wearing extra garments disqualified. Likewise, if something interposed between his flesh and the tunic or the breeches, he is disqualified, for the Merciful One said (ibid. 6), 'He shall put it on his flesh': nothing may interpose between the garments and his flesh. Therefore a priest would not put on the arm Tefillin during the service, because they interpose between the garment and his flesh. He would, however, put on the head Tefillin, because they rest on his hair which is visible between the forehead plate and the turban. One still lacking atonement. For example, a man or woman with a flux, a person afflicted with the scriptural skin impurity, or a woman after childbirth, whose purification has been completed but who have not brought their offerings. We find that the Merciful One wrote concerning a woman after childbirth (ibid. 12), 'The priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be pure,' implying that until then she is impure. The same applies to all other impure people who require an offering: they remain in their impurity until they bring their atonement, with respect to eating sacred offerings and entering the Sanctuary. One who has not washed his hands and feet. Because 'an everlasting statute' is said concerning the sanctification of the hands and feet, and 'an everlasting statute' is said concerning the priestly garments: just as someone who served without the required garments disqualified the offering, so someone who served without washing his hands and feet disqualified it. The order for sanctifying the hands and feet is neither standing upright nor sitting, but leaning forward. He places his right hand on his right foot and his left hand on his left foot, and rubs his feet with his hands as he sanctifies them. He may not sanctify them inside the laver itself, but only from the water coming out of it, for it says (Shmos 30), 'Aharon and his sons shall wash from it'—not inside it. All waters are valid for this sanctification, even if they are not living spring water. An uncircumcised man. If he performed the service, he disqualified the offering. For it is written (in Yechezkel 44), 'Every apostate, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh.' The uncircumcised man is compared to the apostate: just as an apostate who served disqualified the offering, so too an uncircumcised man. Someone sitting. For it is written (Devarim 18), 'To stand to minister': service must be performed standing. Standing on utensils. Since the courtyard pavement sanctifies, and service vessels sanctify what touches them, just as nothing may interpose between the object and a service vessel, so nothing may interpose between the priest and the pavement. Not only utensils, which are not flesh, certainly interpose, but even an animal, which is flesh. And not only an animal, which is not human, but even his fellow's feet, which are human, interpose. If he received with the left hand, he disqualified it. For it is written (Vayikra 4), 'The priest shall take from the blood of the sin offering with his finger and shall put.' This teaches that neither receiving the blood nor applying it may be done except with the right hand. Wherever 'hand' or 'finger' is stated, it means the right, as is learned from the person afflicted with the scriptural skin impurity, concerning whom it is written (ibid. 14), 'The priest shall dip his right finger.' Rabbi Shimon declares it valid. He holds that the verse is expounded in relation to what follows, but not what precedes. Thus 'finger' refers to 'shall put,' written after it, but not to 'shall take,' written before it. The Sages hold that the verse is expounded in relation to both what precedes and what follows: when 'finger' is written, it refers to both, the taking before it and the applying after it. The law follows the Sages. It spilled onto the pavement. The blood had not been received in a vessel. He gathered it up: it is invalid. For it is written (ibid. 16), 'He shall take from the blood of the bull.' What does 'from the blood of the bull' mean? If you suppose that even part of the blood [is enough], it is written (ibid. 4), 'He shall pour out all the blood of the bull'; evidently he must receive all the blood. Rather, read it: 'He shall take blood from the bull'—he must receive it from the bull, not from the ground. A letter is removed from one word and added to another word, and the expression is expounded accordingly. He put it on the ramp, [or on the altar] not opposite the foundation: it is invalid. Nevertheless, the owners have obtained atonement [when the blood has reached the altar]; only the flesh may not be eaten. For the Merciful One said concerning blood (ibid. 17), 'I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement': once blood has reached the altar, the owners have obtained atonement. He put blood assigned below. Below the red line which encircled the altar at its middle. The blood applications made within the upper five cubits, above the line, are called the applications above; those made within the lower five cubits, below the line, are called the applications below. Those assigned inside. Their blood requires sprinkling on the golden altar. Outside. On the outer altar. Invalid. It is forbidden to eat. There is no liability to excision. Someone who eats the flesh of sacred offerings whose blood was disqualified by these defects is not punished with excision.

notes.he: הרע״ב מבחין בין כפרת הבעלים ובין היתר אכילת הבשר. יש לקרוא את ״נתכפרו הבעלים״ עם ״הבשר אינו נאכל״, ולא כהכשר גמור.
notes.en: Bartenura distinguishes atonement for the owners from permission to eat the flesh. “The owners have obtained atonement” must be read together with “the flesh may not be eaten,” not as complete validity.

notes.he: הכבש והנתינה שלא כנגד היסוד נקראים כאן כשני מקרים נפרדים; הקישור שבסוגריים המרובעים מבאר את הלשון המקוצרת. כפרת הבעלים מתבארת בכך שהדם הגיע למזבח, בלי היתר לאכילת הבשר. התנאי שבסוגריים בתרגום נלקח מנימוק זה. אין מכאן הכרעה אם נתינה על הכבש בלבד נחשבת הגעת דם למזבח.
notes.en: Ramp placement and placement not opposite the foundation are read here as separate cases; the bracketed link explains the compact wording. The owners' atonement is explained by the blood having reached the altar, without permission to eat the flesh. The bracketed condition in the translation comes from that reason. This does not settle whether placement on the ramp alone counts as blood reaching the altar.

notes.he: ״בן נכר״ מתפרש כאן במובן דתי: מי מתוך בני ישראל שמעשיו נתנכרו לאביו שבשמים, ״משומד״ בלשון רש״י, ולא אדם מארץ זרה. זהו המובן של apostate בתרגום; מצודת דוד מבדיל במפורש בין מובן זה ובין איש מגויי הארצות. אין לזהות בשל כך כל ערל בשר עם משומד: רש״י מזכיר בנפרד כהן שמתו אחיו מחמת מילה. ההשוואה נוגעת לפסול העבודה האמור כאן, ואינה מפרטת את כל גדרי משומד או את כל דיני המילה.
notes.en: Here 'apostate' renders בן נכר in a religious, not national, sense: someone within Israel whose deeds have become alienated from his Father in heaven. Rashi explicitly calls this person an apostate, and Metzudas David distinguishes this sense from a person of a foreign nation. This does not identify every man uncircumcised in flesh as an apostate: Rashi separately mentions a priest whose brothers died as a result of circumcision. The comparison concerns the service disqualification stated here; it is not a comprehensive definition of apostasy or an account of all circumcision laws.

notes.he: בפירוש המלא ההפניה היא ויקרא כב; בפירוש היומי כתוב ויקרא כג.
notes.en: The full commentary cites Vayikra 22; the daily commentary prints Vayikra 23.

entries.english: Someone who slaughters the sacrifice. A peace offering or another kind that is eaten. An olive's bulk of the skin of the fat tail. This teaches that the skin of the fat tail is not treated like the fat tail itself. He is thus intending to eat something normally eaten, and the offering is therefore disqualified. If it were treated like the fat tail itself, he would be intending to eat something normally burned on the altar, and the offering would not be disqualified, as we learn immediately below: to eat something normally eaten, or to burn something normally burned, disqualifies it. He is not punished with excision. The person who eats it; even if he eats outside, he is not punished with excision. To eat its flesh tomorrow. This cannot be explained as referring to a peace offering, but rather to a thanksgiving offering or a sin offering. For a peace offering, tomorrow is still its proper time. But for dashing its blood or burning its sacrificial fats, tomorrow is beyond its proper time even for a peace offering. An offering invalidated by out-of-time intent, for which there is liability to excision. The person who eats it is punished with excision even if he eats it within its proper time.

notes.he: ״למחר״ באכילה מתפרש בתודה וחטאת, לא בשלמים. לעומת זאת, בזריקת הדם ובהקטרת האימורים גם בשלמים למחר הוא חוץ לזמן.
notes.en: “Tomorrow” for eating is explained as a thanksgiving offering or sin offering, not a peace offering. For dashing blood and burning sacrificial fats, however, tomorrow is out of time even for a peace offering.

notes.he: בדיבור המלא נאמר פיגול, ובדיבור היומי נאמר פסול עם חיוב כרת.
notes.en: The full lemma says an offering invalidated by out-of-time intent; the daily lemma says disqualified while also stating excision liability.

entries.english: One who slaughters, receives, carries, or dashes. If, while occupied with one of these four services, he thought about the sacrifice that he would eat something from it normally eaten, namely the flesh, or burn something from it normally burned, namely the sacrificial fats, outside its proper place, the flesh is forbidden to eat, but someone who eats it is not punished with excision. If he thought about the sacrifice that he would eat it beyond its proper time, the sacrifice is invalidated by out-of-time intent, and someone who eats it is punished with excision even within its proper time. For it is written (Vayikra 7), 'If any of the flesh of his peace sacrifice is indeed eaten on the third day, it shall not be accepted; the one offering it shall not have it reckoned to him; it shall be an invalidated offering.' The verse speaks of someone intending to eat of his sacrifice on the third day. Or does it speak only of someone actually eating of his sacrifice on the third day? You must ask in astonishment: after it was valid, can it become invalid again? Moreover, it says, 'It shall not be reckoned': it is disqualified by thought, and is not disqualified on the third day. From the verse's doubled expression, 'eaten, eaten,' we expound that Scripture speaks of two kinds of eating: one is human eating, namely the flesh, and one is the altar's eating, namely the sacrificial fats. Of both it says, 'It shall not be reckoned; it shall be an invalidated offering.' Provided that the permitting element is offered. The blood, which permits [the flesh]. As prescribed. [As though it were valid,] with no other disqualification. If, however, it has another disqualifying intent, it is removed from the category of an offering invalidated by out-of-time intent, as will be explained. Concerning such an offering it says, 'It shall not be accepted,' just as acceptance is stated concerning a valid offering. This teaches that the process of acceptance for an offering with out-of-time intent corresponds to that of a valid offering. Just as a valid offering's acceptance is not called acceptance until the blood is dashed, the last of the four permitting services, so the out-of-time status is not settled but remains pending until the blood is dashed, the conclusion of all the permitting services.

notes.he: ״כאילו היה כשר״ אינו אומר שהקרבן מותר באכילה. ההשוואה לכשר נוגעת להשלמת ארבע העבודות בלי פסול אחר, עד זריקת הדם.
notes.en: “As though it were valid” does not mean that the offering may be eaten. The comparison with a valid offering concerns completion of the four services without another defect, through the dashing of the blood.

notes.he: הפירוש היומי חסר את הרחבת ״במחשבה הוא נפסל״ ואת דרשת שתי האכילות שבפירוש המלא.
notes.en: The daily commentary lacks the full discussion of invalidation by thought and the derivation of two kinds of eating.

entries.english: Without disqualifying intent. Without a thought that disqualifies. The Passover offering and the sin offering which he slaughtered not for their own designation. This removes them from the category of an offering invalidated by out-of-time intent. With other sacrifices, however, service not for their own designation does not remove them from that category, because they remain valid when offered not for their own designation.

notes.he: שלא לשמה מוציא מפיגול בפסח ובחטאת מפני שהוא פוסל אותם. בשאר זבחים הוא אינו פוסל באותו אופן, ולכן אין ללמוד מהם שהפיגול נפקע.
notes.en: Wrong designation removes the out-of-time status for the Passover offering and sin offering because it disqualifies them. Other sacrifices are not disqualified in that way, so one cannot infer that their out-of-time status is removed.

entries.english: To eat an olive's bulk outside and an olive's bulk tomorrow. This is the same rule we have already stated, except that the earlier clause deals with two services: he slaughtered intending to eat an olive's bulk outside and received the blood intending to eat an olive's bulk tomorrow. Here it concerns one service: he slaughtered intending to eat an olive's bulk tomorrow and an olive's bulk outside. Rabbi Yehudah says, etc. He disagrees with the entire Mishna, for he does not hold that another disqualifying intent removes the offering from the category of out-of-time invalidation unless that other disqualification preceded its out-of-time invalidation. He disagrees even within a single service, for he holds: take the first expression as decisive. The law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah. To eat half an olive's bulk and to burn half an olive's bulk. Both are beyond their proper time, or both outside their proper place. Valid, because eating and burning do not combine. To disqualify it. Here there is not the required quantity, and there too there is not the required quantity.

notes.he: הפירוש מחיל את מחלוקת רבי יהודה גם על עבודה אחת, לפי הקדמת הלשון. בסוף נאמר במפורש שאין הלכה כרבי יהודה.
notes.en: The commentary applies Rabbi Yehudah’s disagreement even to a single service, according to the first expression. It ends by stating expressly that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah.

entries.english: The impure person who went down to immerse. In his uncertainty he is impure: leave the person in his established status, which is a status of impurity.

notes.he: החזקה שייכת לאדם שהיה טמא לפני הירידה. עצם הירידה למים אינה מכריעה אם התקיימה טבילה כשרה.
notes.en: The established status belongs to the person who was impure before descending. Entering the water alone does not settle whether a valid immersion occurred.

entries.english: Whether in a private domain or in a public domain, they are impure. Although a case of doubtful impurity in a public domain is pure, this is uncertainty about purification, not uncertainty about contracting impurity. In a case of severe impurity. Through a primary source of impurity which makes him impure by Torah law. Lighter impurity. Rabbinic impurity. He ate impure foods. If he ate half a loaf-portion of impure foods or drank a quarter-loag of impure liquids, his body is disqualified from eating the priestly portion, and he disqualifies the priestly portion by rabbinic law. These are all among the eighteen matters on which the Sages decreed, and they are all explained in the first chapter of Shabbos. Even if he immersed. There are now two adverse possibilities: perhaps he did not immerse at all, and even if he immersed, perhaps the pool became deficient before the immersion. Nevertheless, in his uncertainty he is pure. Rabbi Yose declares him impure. Even in a case of rabbinic impurity, because the person has an established status of impurity. But where the uncertainty is whether he became impure or imparted impurity. For example, it is uncertain whether he ate impure foods or did not eat them: this is uncertainty about becoming impure. Or he certainly ate impure foods, but it is uncertain whether he touched a loaf of the priestly portion or did not touch it: this is uncertainty about imparting impurity. In these cases Rabbi Yose declares pure, because here there is no established status of impurity. The law does not follow Rabbi Yose.

notes.he: רבי יוסי מטהר כשאין חזקת טומאה קודמת לדבר המסופק: ספק אכילה ביחס לאדם, וספק נגיעה ביחס לתרומה. אין זו סתירה להחמרתו בהסרת טומאה ידועה.
notes.en: Rabbi Yose declares pure where the subject of the doubt has no prior established impurity: doubtful eating for the person, and doubtful contact for the priestly portion. This does not contradict his stringency about removal of known impurity.

entries.english: The uncertainty about drawn water which the Sages declared pure. In tractate Taharos, in the chapter 'One who throws impurity,' we learn there: These are the doubtful cases which the Sages declared pure—uncertainty about drawn water for an immersion pool. It is uncertain whether it fell in. Three loag of drawn water into a deficient immersion pool. It is uncertain whether there were forty se'uh in it.
