That is, it is uncertain whether the pool had forty se'uh of valid water before the drawn water fell in, in which case drawn water no longer disqualifies it. There is a basis for attribution. There is a way to attribute their fall so that they caused no disqualification. There is no basis for attribution. Whichever way you consider it, whichever pool they fell into, they disqualified it; therefore both are disqualified. The reason we declare the doubtful drawn water pure here when there is a basis for attribution is that the drawn-water restriction is rabbinic. As for what is taught in Toras Kohanim, 'But a spring and a cistern, a gathering of water'—just as a spring is made by Heaven, so an immersion pool must be made by Heaven—this is merely a scriptural support.

notes.he: כאן הפירוש מנמק את ההקלה בכך שפסול השאובים דרבנן, ואת הדרשה הוא מכנה אסמכתא. זו קביעת הפירוש המקומי, ולא היתר גורף לכל ספק במקואות.
notes.en: Here the commentary grounds leniency in the rabbinic drawn-water restriction and calls the derivation scriptural support. This is the local commentary’s claim, not a blanket permission for every doubtful immersion pool.

entries.english: At the outset. There was no water at all in the immersion pool when a quarter-loag of drawn water fell into it, and afterward its required quantity was completed with rainwater. Onto the water. After it already contained much valid water. The Sages say. The law follows the Sages.

notes.he: רביעית שנפלה לבור ריק היא תחילת המקרה, והשלמת השיעור במי גשמים באה אחריה. ״על פני המים״ הוא מצב אחר, שכבר היו בו מים כשרים.
notes.en: The case starts with a quarter-loag falling into an empty pool, followed by completion with rainwater. “Onto the water” is a different situation, with valid water already present.

entries.english: One loag in each. One loag in every hollow. Before it reached the third hollow, it is valid. It is like a complete immersion pool into which three loag of drawn water fell, which do not disqualify it. Here too, since the pool contained forty se'uh before the water reached the third hollow, the pool was not disqualified. Like an immersion pool beside another. Like a valid immersion pool beside a drawn-water pool: this one remains valid, and that one remains disqualified. Here too, the water in the hollows is regarded as standing independently, not as mixed together. The law does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

notes.he: לרבי שמעון מי הגומות אינם נחשבים מעורבים. הפירוש מסיים שאין הלכה כמותו, ואין לייחס את ההפרדה הזאת לדעת התנא הראשון.
notes.en: For Rabbi Shimon, the water in the hollows is not considered mixed. The commentary ends by rejecting his ruling; this separate-water treatment must not be attributed to the first opinion.

entries.english: One who pushes aside. Like 'one who removes': he moves the mud to one side. It does not mean that he lifted the mud out of the water; rather, he moved it aside while it was still in the water. For if he lifted it out of the water, it is regarded as drawn, and if three loag flow from it, they disqualify the immersion pool. It is specifically when the pool does not contain forty se'uh that three loag of drawn water disqualify it. If it already contained forty se'uh, all the drawn water in the world does not disqualify it. Rabbi Shimon declares it valid. Because he does not intend to draw water, but only to move the mud to one place. The law does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

notes.he: הגבלת שלושה לוגים נאמרת במקוה חסר. הפירוש מבדיל במפורש מקוה שכבר היו בו ארבעים סאה לפני נפילת השאובים.
notes.en: The three-loag disqualification concerns a deficient pool. The commentary expressly distinguishes a pool which already had forty se’uh before the drawn water entered.

entries.english: To dry them. The translation of 'And behold, they had dried' is 'And behold, they had become dry.' It is specifically to dry them: he did not intend to collect water, so the water did not become drawn. For it is written [Vayikra 11], 'But a spring and a cistern': just as a spring involves no human handling, so a cistern must involve no human handling. If it is a rainy period. The skies became covered with clouds and rain fell. If there is a little water in the cistern. This is the reading; we do not read 'or.' He may break them. The jars, so that the water inside them falls into the cistern. This is channeling water along a course, since it falls into the cistern from broken vessels. Otherwise. It is not a rainy period; alternatively, there is no water in the cistern. He may not break them. If it is not a rainy period, he cannot make an immersion pool from the water in the jars alone, for Rabbi Eliezer holds that drawn water conveyed along a course is invalid [when it makes up all or most of the pool]. But when it is a rainy period, he may break them to channel this water, and most of the pool will be filled with rainwater. When there is no water at all in it, he may not break them even in a rainy period, lest a quarter-loag of the water fall into the cistern before the breaking. Rabbi Eliezer follows his own position stated above: a quarter-loag of water disqualifies the immersion pool (as an initial practice) [at the outset]. Rabbi Yehoshua says: In either case he may break them. He holds that three loag disqualify an immersion pool, whether at the outset or at the end, and not a quarter-loag. We do not fear that three loag will fall into the cistern before the breaking. Even if it is not a rainy period, he may break them, for he can channel enough to make the required quantity of an immersion pool: he holds that drawn water which has all been channeled along a course is pure. The law does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. Or turn them over. He overturns the jars on the roof so that the water will not fall from them into the cistern, but will fall to another side and flow from there into the cistern. But he may not pour them out. If he lifted the jars and poured them out, the water would become like drawn water, since it involves human handling.

notes.he: שתי הצורות ״לכתחלה״ ו״בתחלה״ אינן זהות: הראשונה עשויה לציין הנהגה מראש, והשנייה את הבור הריק. כאן הטעם קשור לרביעית הנופלת לפני השבירה ולדעת רבי אליעזר.
notes.en: The two forms “as an initial practice” and “at the outset” are not identical: the former may describe a prospective practice, the latter the empty pool. Here the reason concerns a quarter-loag falling before the breaking and Rabbi Eliezer’s position.

notes.he: כאן הפירוש גורס ״אם״ ולא ״או״: לרבי אליעזר נדרשים גם גשמים וגם מעט מים בבור.
notes.en: Here the commentary reads “if,” not “or”: Rabbi Eliezer requires both rain and a little water in the cistern.

notes.he: הציטוט היומי קצר מן הפירוש המלא: חסרים בו ההיתר בעונת גשמים, מילוי רוב המקוה במי גשמים, וחזרת האיסור כשאין בבור מים כלל.
notes.en: The daily quotation is shorter than the complete commentary: it omits the rainy-period permission, the pool's being filled mostly with rainwater, and the renewed prohibition when there is no water at all in the cistern.

notes.he: ״לכתחלה״ בסוגריים עגולים ו״בתחלה״ במרובעים הן שתי צורות שונות במקור.
notes.en: The source carries two distinct forms: “as an initial practice” in parentheses and “at the outset” in square brackets.

entries.english: The plasterer. A craftsman who plasters the cistern with lime so that it will retain its water. He usually brings the lime into the cistern in a pot. That cistern contained valid water, and the pot sank into the water and filled. If the water stands above it by any amount, he may break it. The water has not been drawn, because it is continuously joined together. If, however, he lifted the pot with his hand, the water would be cut off and become detached. Otherwise. The water does not stand above it. He may not break it. This deals with a time that is not rainy. If it were a rainy period, then since there is water in the cistern, he could break it, as we said. Rabbi Yehoshua says: In either case he may break it. Because he can channel the water along a course, as we explained above.

notes.he: העמדת המקרה שלא בעונת גשמים נוגעת לאיסור רבי אליעזר כשאין מים מעל העציץ. בעונת גשמים וכשיש מים בבור הוא עצמו מתיר לפי הפירוש.
notes.en: The non-rainy-period qualification concerns Rabbi Eliezer’s prohibition when water does not stand above the pot. In a rainy period, with water in the cistern, he himself permits it according to the commentary.

entries.english: Someone arranges jars in the cistern and they fill, even though the cistern absorbed its water. There is no water left in the cistern except what is in the jars. He may break them. This follows Rabbi Yehoshua, for whom a quarter-loag does not disqualify. He breaks the jars and makes an immersion pool from the outset.

notes.he: הפירוש תולה את ההיתר ברבי יהושע, שאינו פוסל ברביעית. אין להסיק מכאן שרבי אליעזר מתיר להתחיל בור ריק באותם תנאים.
notes.en: The commentary attributes the permission to Rabbi Yehoshua, who does not disqualify with a quarter-loag. It does not imply that Rabbi Eliezer permits starting an empty pool under the same conditions.

entries.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says: In the mud and in the water. When water stands above the mud, Rabbi Yehoshua permits immersion even if his feet sink into the mud, because the water comes first. Rabbi Eliezer does not accept this reasoning. If, however, he were immersing a small utensil in the water standing above the mud, Rabbi Eliezer concedes that its immersion is effective, since it does not sink into the mud at all, and the mud combines to complete forty se'uh. The law follows Rabbi Yehoshua. A reed sinks by itself. It is so soft and dissolved that if a reed is put in it, the reed sinks into the mud by itself. A place where a measuring reed will not remain standing. A reed used for measuring does not stand by itself in it. This mud is not as soft and dissolved as the first kind. A plumb weight. The builders' tin weight. Each of all these measures adds to the mud's hardness and thickness: the first is the softest of all, the second harder than it, the third harder than that, and so on through them all. Through the mouth of a barrel. Its mouth is narrow and small. If the mud is so soft that it can be poured and enter the narrow mouth of a barrel, immersion in it is effective. The waterskin's tube. A reed tube placed at the opening of the waterskin into which water is poured. The hole of the waterskin's tube is large enough for two medium fingers to turn around in it: the breadth of the first two fingers of the hand, not the thumb. Measured in a loag vessel. As long as it is soft enough to be measured in a loag vessel, which is a vessel holding six eggs, it is counted together with the immersion pool, and one may immerse in it. The law follows Rabbi Yehudah.

notes.he: הודאת רבי אליעזר נאמרת בכלי קטן שאינו שוקע בטיט כלל. ההלכה כרבי יהושע במחלוקת הטבילה, וכרבי יהודה במבחן רכות הטיט; אלו שתי הכרעות שונות.
notes.en: Rabbi Eliezer’s concession concerns a small utensil which does not sink into the mud at all. The law follows Rabbi Yehoshua on immersion, and Rabbi Yehudah on the mud-softness test; these are separate rulings.

notes.he: במשפט על הכלי הקטן הציטוט היומי אומר ״הצים״, ואילו הפירוש המלא אומר ״הצפים״, כלומר המים שמעל הטיט.
notes.en: In the small-utensil sentence the daily quotation has the defective word הצים; the complete commentary has הצפים, referring to the water above the mud.

notes.he: בתיאור המבחנים הפירוש המלא אומר ״שהראשון רך מכולם״ ו״וכן כולם״; בציטוט היומי חסרה ״רך״ ונאמר ״וכל כולם״.
notes.en: In describing the tests, the complete commentary says the first is the softest of all and continues “and so with all of them.” The daily quotation lacks “soft” and has a different, defective closing phrase.

notes.he: הכרעה כרבי יהושע בראש הפירוש אינה זהה להכרעה כרבי יהודה בסופו.
notes.en: The ruling for Rabbi Yehoshua near the start is not the same ruling as the one for Rabbi Yehudah at the end.
